Prioritize your goals and timeline each one separately. If your secondary goals limit your ability to reach the primary goal then deal with it - drop it off the list or figure out how to accomplish it without messing with your primary objective.

Unless you have for sure found the girl, don't sweat getting married in 4 years. You'll just end up settling and miserable in 5 years.

As far as "make money" there is no guarantee a degree will help you get there, maybe you could change that one a little to be "In 4 years, I would like to have 'x' amount of money in the bank." That way, you can break it down to how much you need to start setting aside, beginning with tomorrow.

Anyway, state your goals, the time limit to achieve them, then work backwards in time. You can break down into each year, each month, etc. It's easier to start with the 3rd year overall, 2nd year every 6 months, 1.5 years every month, and 6 months from now by the week down to every day this month (hope that makes sense). Once you get down to tomorrow, you'll have a list of a few things you need to do each day for a few weeks. This way your goals won't seem overwhelming because you'll see tomorrow's list and think, "Fuck, this will be easy."

After those first few weeks, the longer time spans in the future will be easy to tackle, because you'll have developed the habit of taking small steps every day to reach your goals in the future. If there are any slip-ups, those time-frames are a good time to look at your goals and rethink strategy.

In this process, you will have to research your options (degree programs, job outlook, savings plans, learning about yourself to find someone compatible), and choose whichever fits your life best. But, if you change in the future (if you're under 25, you'll probably change), you will already know of different options to keep on a similar path.

Write all this crap down and show your dad (the timeline thing). This was advice from my dad when I was in my early 20's and felt totally lost, only I did an 8-year plan instead of 4, and it worked for me.

Start your plan from the end and work backwards.

Pick the thing that you want to accomplish and work back from there.

"I want to make it to work on time tomorrow at 5am. That means I have to wake up at 4 and take a shower and get dressed in time to drive to work and be there by 5. If I have to be up by 4, that means that I have to go to bed around 7pm the night before so that I get enough sleep to be effective at work. Before I go to bed I should eat something so that I can sleep well. Then I should have a good day at work tomorrow."

Pick a goal and work backwards from it to the present. Break it down into smaller pieces that you can act on in the present.

Think of your life as constructing a building... You have to know what the building is going to look like in the end, but you can't just make that building appear by magic. First you have to grade the land and make it flat. Then you have to pour the slab. Then you have to start stacking bricks. Then you have put the roof on. Eventually you have that building that you pictured.

Or think about it like baking a cake. You can just throw all of the ingredients in a pan and throw it in the oven... Before you bake it you have to make the batter. Before that you have to sift the flour and crack the eggs in a procedure to get the right results.

The more intricate you make the plan working backward the easier it will be to reach your goal.

TL;DR

“We conclude that Canada has not fulfilled its duty to consult,” according to the ruling.

“The inadequacies — more than just a handful and more than mere imperfections — left entire subjects of central interest to the affected First Nations, sometimes subjects affecting their subsistence and well-being, entirely ignored.”

Followed by

“Based on our view of the totality of the evidence, we are satisfied that Canada failed in Phase IV to engage, dialogue and grapple with the concerns expressed to it in good faith by all of the applicant/appellant First Nations,” the court noted.

“Missing was any indication of an intention to amend or supplement the conditions imposed by the Joint Review Panel, to correct any errors or omissions in its Report, or to provide meaningful feedback in response to the material concerns raised. Missing was a real and sustained effort to pursue meaningful two-way dialogue. Missing was someone from Canada’s side empowered to do more than take notes, someone able to respond meaningfully at some point.”
